claims.text: High-temperature structural stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by the interplay of configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and solid-solution-phase formation.
The initial nanoparticles possess an FCC or BCC lattice.
In situ XRD and TEM can provide information about nanoparticle stability during high-temperature exposure.
Atomistic simulations can provide mechanistic insight into high-temperature nanoparticle formation or stability.
Characterization and simulation-based validation constitute an intervention capable of changing nanoparticle stability.
Temperature and oxygen partial pressure influence phase stability.
Configurational entropy is a structural mediator of nanoparticle stability.
Lattice distortion is a structural mediator of nanoparticle stability.
Increased configurational entropy stabilizes a solid-solution phase.
Increased lattice distortion stabilizes a solid-solution phase.
Entropy and lattice-distortion stabilization prevent phase segregation.
Entropy and lattice-distortion stabilization prevent intermetallic-phase formation.
The proposed intervention will improve structural and chemical stability under high-temperature service.
Stability will increase by at least 20% relative to baseline.
The hypothesis applies from 773 to 1923 K.
The hypothesis applies at oxygen partial pressures from 10^-5 to 10^-1 atm.
The relationship among configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and stability may depend on nanoparticle composition and structure.
Failure to maintain the solid-solution phase under high-temperature exposure would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: In situ characterization and simulation validation are observational or epistemic procedures, not material changes expected to alter entropy, lattice distortion, or phase stability. Comparing characterized particles with particles 'without characterization' therefore does not provide a coherent causal baseline for the predicted stability improvement.

The predicted increase and falsification threshold use percentages of an undefined stability metric; moreover, outcomes between a 20% increase and a 10% decrease are not assigned a decisive interpretation.
